claim: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are indispensable for maintaining self-tolerance by suppressing conventional T cells.
source: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are indispensable for maintaining self-tolerance by suppressing conventional T cells.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in immunology, supported by extensive literature and the context of the study.

claim: Tregs promote tumor growth by inhibiting anticancer immunity.
source: On the other hand, Tregs promote tumor growth by inhibiting anticancer immunity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Togashi et al., 2019 in the Introduction section.

claim: Tregs increase the quorum of self-reactive CD8+ T cells required for the induction of experimental autoimmune diabetes in mice.
source: In this study, we identified that Tregs increase the quorum of self-reactive CD8+ T cells required for the induction of experimental autoimmune diabetes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2, demonstrating that Treg depletion reduces the number of OT-I T cells needed to induce diabetes.

claim: The major suppression mechanism of Tregs is limiting available IL-2.
source: Their major suppression mechanism is limiting available IL-2, an essential T-cell cytokine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing increased IL-2 signaling in the absence of Tregs and that excess IL-2 phenocopies Treg depletion.

claim: Tregs inhibit the formation of a previously uncharacterized subset of antigen-stimulated KLRK1+ IL-7R+ (KILR) CD8+ effector T cells.
source: Specifically, Tregs inhibit the formation of a previously uncharacterized subset of antigen-stimulated KLRK1+ IL-7R+ (KILR) CD8+ effector T cells, which are distinct from conventional effector CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data in Figure 5 showing that KILR cells occur almost exclusively in the absence of Tregs.

claim: KILR CD8+ T cells show superior cell-killing abilities in vivo.
source: KILR CD8+ T cells show superior cell-killing abilities in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo killing assay data shown in Figure 6H demonstrating enhanced cytotoxic activity of KLRK1+ T cells.

claim: The administration of agonistic IL-2 immunocomplexes phenocopies the absence of Tregs.
source: The administration of agonistic IL-2 immunocomplexes phenocopies the absence of Tregs, i.e., it induces KILR CD8+ T cells, promotes autoimmunity, and enhances antitumor responses in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4E-H (autoimmunity) and Figure 7 (antitumor responses).

claim: Counterparts of KILR CD8+ T cells were found in human blood.
source: Counterparts of KILR CD8+ T cells were found in the human blood, revealing them as a potential target for immunotherapy.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of human CD8+ T cell atlas data shown in Figure 6I-L.

claim: The absence of Tregs in FOXP3-deficient individuals leads to immunodysregulation polyendocrinopathy enteropathy X-linked syndrome.
source: The absence of Tregs in FOXP3-deficient individuals leads to a severe autoimmune condition called immunodysregulation polyendocrinopathy enteropathy X-linked syndrome (Bennett et al., 2001; Brunkow et al., 2001; Wildin et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by three citations to published literature.

claim: At steady state, Tregs suppress the proliferation of CD8+ T cells.
source: At steady state, Tregs suppress the proliferation of CD8+ T cells (Chinen et al., 2016) and prevent the spontaneous differentiation of memory CD8+ T cells into effector cells (Laidlaw et al., 2015; Kalia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Tregs suppress antigenic responses of CD8+ T cells.
source: Moreover, Tregs suppress antigenic responses of CD8+ T cells (McNally et al., 2011; Kastenmuller et al., 2011; Pace et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Multiple mechanisms of Treg-mediated suppression of CD8+ T cells have been proposed, including reducing expression of co-stimulatory molecules on APCs via CTLA4.
source: Multiple mechanisms of Treg-mediated suppression of CD8+ T cells have been proposed, such as reducing the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on antigen-presenting cells (APC) via CTLA4 (Kalia et al., 2015; Kastenmuller et al., 2011; Schildknecht et al., 2010), limiting the availability of IL-2 (McNally et al., 2011; Kastenmuller et al., 2011), production of anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 (Laidlaw et al., 2015) and TGFβ (Green et al., 2003), and limiting the production of CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 chemokines by APCs (Pace et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The induction of diabetes in the majority of Treg-replete mice required 10^6 adoptively transferred OT-I T cells followed by priming with OVA peptide and LPS.
source: The induction of diabetes in the majority of Treg-replete mice required 106 adoptively transferred OT-I T cells followed by priming with OVA peptide and LPS (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: After the depletion of Tregs, the number of transferred OT-I T cells sufficient to induce diabetes in the vast majority of animals dropped dramatically.
source: After the depletion of Tregs, the number of transferred OT-I T cells, sufficient to induce diabetes in the vast majority of animals, dropped dramatically (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased glucose levels in the urine and blood are preceded by abnormal morphology of the pancreatic islets and loss of insulin production together with the infiltration of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in the islets on day 4 post immunization.
source: We observed that increased glucose levels in the urine and blood are preceded by abnormal morphology of the pancreatic islets and loss of insulin production together with the infiltration of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in the islets on day 4 post immunization (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The expansion of OT-I T cells in the spleen was enhanced in Treg-deficient mice compared with Treg-replete mice.
source: Accordingly, the expansion of OT-I T cells in the spleen was enhanced in Treg-deficient mice compared with Treg-replete mice (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F and supplementary figures.

claim: When 10^6 OT-I T cells were transferred, 50% of Treg-depleted mice developed diabetes even though they were primed with LPS alone without the cognate peptide.
source: When 106 OT-I T cells were transferred, 50% of Treg-depleted mice developed diabetes, even though they were primed with LPS alone without the cognate peptide (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The small amount of endogenous OVA was sufficient to prime OT-I T cells in the absence of Tregs.
source: This was possible because the small amount of endogenous OVA was sufficient to prime OT-I T cells in the absence of Tregs, as revealed by more robust expansion and CD44+ CD62L- effector T-cell formation in Foxp3DTR RIP.OVA than in Foxp3DTR mice (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing Foxp3DTR RIP.OVA and Foxp3DTR mice shown in Figure 1H.

claim: As few as 10^3 transferred OT-I T cells were able to induce autoimmune diabetes in RIP.OVA mice upon DC-OVA priming.
source: In contrast to OVA peptide and LPS priming, as few as 103 transferred OT-I T cells were able to induce autoimmune diabetes in RIP.OVA mice upon DC-OVA priming (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When 3 × 10^2 OT-I T cells were transferred, all Treg-depleted mice, but only one third of Treg-replete mice, were diabetic.
source: When 3 × 102 OT-I T cells were transferred, all Treg-depleted mice, but only one third of Treg-replete mice, were diabetic (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The absence of Tregs increased the susceptibility to diabetes upon priming with DC-Q4R7.
source: Accordingly, the absence of Tregs increased the susceptibility to diabetes upon priming with DC-Q4R7, although as many as 3 × 104 OT-I T cells were required to induce diabetes in most Treg-depleted hosts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treg-replete RIP.OVA mice were resistant to 10^6 OT-I T cells primed with DC-Q4H7, whereas most Treg-depleted mice manifested diabetes.
source: Along this line, Treg-replete RIP.OVA mice were resistant to 106 OT-I T cells primed with DC-Q4H7, whereas most Treg-depleted mice manifested diabetes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expansion of OT-I T cells, their expression of IL-2Rα (CD25) and KLRG1, and the absolute number of KLRG1+ OT-I T cells in the spleen were greater in Treg-depleted mice than in Treg-replete RIP.OVA mice on day 6 post-immunization with DC-OVA, -Q4R7, or -Q4H7.
source: The expansion of OT-I T cells, their expression of IL-2Rα (CD25; a subunit of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor) and KLRG1 (a marker of short-lived effector cells), and the absolute number of KLRG1+ OT-I T cells in the spleen were greater in Treg-depleted mice than in Treg-replete RIP.OVA mice on day 6 post-immunization with DC-OVA, -Q4R7, or -Q4H7 (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D-F and supplementary figures.

claim: Tregs increase the quorum of self-reactive CD8+ T cells required for inducing autoimmune diabetes, irrespective of the affinity of the priming antigen.
source: Collectively, these results showed that Tregs increase the quorum of self-reactive CD8+ T cells required for inducing autoimmune diabetes, irrespective of the affinity of the priming antigen.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data from Figure 2 showing Treg effects across different antigen affinities.

claim: Expanded Tregs prevented DC-OVA-induced diabetes in most animals.
source: We observed that the expanded Tregs prevented DC-OVA-induced diabetes in most animals (Figure 2H), showing that enhancing the overall Treg activity increases self-tolerance and prevents the induction of the experimental diabetes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H using IL-2ic to expand Tregs.

claim: Conventional CD4+ T cells increased the incidence of experimental diabetes and accelerated its onset.
source: We observed that conventional CD4+ T cells, albeit presumably tolerant to OVA, increased the incidence of experimental diabetes and accelerated its onset (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, C and supplementary figures.

claim: Tregs reduced the incidence of diabetes compared with mice receiving no CD4+ T cells.
source: In contrast, Tregs reduced the incidence of diabetes compared with mice receiving no CD4+ T cells (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, C and supplementary figures.

claim: Conventional CD4+ T cells enhanced the expansion of OT-I T cells and increased the number of KLRG1+ OT-I T cells, whereas Tregs elicited the opposite effect.
source: Conventional CD4+ T cells enhanced the expansion of OT-I T cells and increased the number of KLRG1+ OT-I T cells, whereas Tregs elicited the opposite effect (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), as revealed on day 8 post-immunization.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D, E and supplementary figures.

claim: Conventional CD4+ T cells provide a bystander help to self-reactive CD8+ T cells, whereas Tregs directly suppress the priming of CD8+ T cells.
source: Overall, these experiments showed that conventional CD4+ T cells provide a bystander help to self-reactive CD8+ T cells, whereas Tregs directly suppress the priming of CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data from Figure 3 showing effects in Cd3e-/- mice lacking endogenous T cells.

claim: Treg depletion increases IL-2 signaling in OT-I T cells, as shown by significantly higher levels of IL-2Rα and pSTAT5 early after priming.
source: We observed significantly higher levels of IL-2Rα and an IL-2 signaling intermediate, pSTAT5 in OT-I T cells in Treg-deficient mice early after priming (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A, B and supplementary figures.

claim: Tregs limit IL-2 signaling in self-reactive CD8+ T cells in vivo.
source: These results showed that Tregs limit IL-2 signaling in self-reactive CD8+ T cells in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation of increased IL-2Rα and pSTAT5 in the absence of Tregs.

claim: Tregs efficiently suppressed proliferation and IL-2Rα expression in CD8+ T cells ex vivo.
source: Tregs efficiently suppressed proliferation and IL-2Rα expression in CD8+ T cells ex vivo (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: An addition of excessive IL-2 abolished Treg-mediated suppression of CD8+ T cells ex vivo.
source: An addition of excessive IL-2 abolished this suppression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both IL-2/JES6 and IL-2/S4B6 immunocomplexes broke the peripheral tolerance and induced the onset of autoimmune diabetes similarly to Treg-depletion.
source: Both clones of IL-2ic broke the peripheral tolerance and induced the onset of autoimmune diabetes similarly to the Treg-depletion (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: IL-2ic promoted the formation of KLRG1+ effector OT-I T cells despite a dramatic IL-2-dependent expansion of Tregs.
source: IL-2ic promoted the formation of KLRG1+ effector OT-I T cells (Figure 4G), despite a dramatic IL-2-dependent expansion of Tregs at the same time (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Tregs are unable to suppress CD8+ T cells in the excess of IL-2 signal.
source: Overall, these results showed that Tregs are unable to suppress CD8+ T cells in the excess of IL-2 signal, although Tregs themselves expand dramatically, which should augment their overall suppressive capacity with the exception of the limiting IL-2 mechanism.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing that IL-2ic induces diabetes despite Treg expansion.

claim: The major mechanism of Treg-mediated suppression of self-reactive CD8+ T cells is the reduction of IL-2 availability.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the major mechanism of Treg-mediated suppression of self-reactive CD8+ T cells is the reduction of IL-2 availability.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including IL-2 signaling data and IL-2ic experiments.

claim: Antigen-activated CD8+ T cells were much more responsive to IL-2 than activated CD4+ T cells.
source: This IL-2-dependent mechanism might be specific for the suppression of CD8+ T cells since antigen-activated CD8+ T cells were much more responsive to IL-2 than activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: IL-2-responsive genes were upregulated in OT-I T cells primed in Treg-depleted mice, including those encoding granzyme B, perforin, and IL-2Rα.
source: IL-2-responsive genes were upregulated in OT-I T cells primed in the Treg-depleted mice, including those encoding the key cytotoxic molecules granzyme B and perforin, as well as IL-2Rα (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of OT-I T cells highlighted five distinct activated subsets.
source: Unsupervised clustering highlighted five distinct activated OT-I T cell subsets (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cluster 4 was characterized by the expression of Klrk1, Gzmb and by overall similarity to the NK cell gene expression profile.
source: Cluster 4, on the other hand, did not match to any established CD8+ T-cell subset. It was characterized by the expression of a natural killer (NK) cell activation receptor gene Klrk1 (alias Nkg2d), Gzmb (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and by the overall similarity to the NK cell gene expression profile (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Cluster 4 cells occurred almost exclusively in the absence of Tregs.
source: Interestingly, these cells occurred almost exclusively in the absence of Tregs (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The larger subset of cluster 4 expressed Il7r, Cd103, and NK cell markers Ifitm1-3 and Cd7, but not Cd49d (Itga4).
source: This cluster could be further divided into two subsets. The larger of them expressed Il7r, Cd103, and NK cell markers Ifitm1-3 and Cd7, but not a typical effector T-cell marker Cd49d (Itga4), which encodes a subunit of the integrin VLA4 (Figure 5F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5F-H and supplementary figures.

claim: KLRK1+ IL-7R+ CD49d- CD8+ T cells are ~20-fold more frequent in the absence of Tregs during the priming than in Treg-replete conditions.
source: This confirmed that KLRK1+ IL-7R+ CD49d- CD8+ T cells are ~20-fold more frequent in the absence of Tregs during the priming than in Treg-replete conditions (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry validation shown in Figure 5I.

claim: KILR effector CD8+ T cells express high levels of cytotoxic molecules such as granzymes.
source: They express high levels of cytotoxic molecules, such as granzymes, but unlike conventional effector CD8+ T cells, they also express high levels of IL-7R.
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq and flow cytometry data showing expression of Gzmb and Il7r in KILR cells.

claim: KILR effector CD8+ T cells express several NK receptors, including KLRK1/NKG2D.
source: Moreover, they express several NK receptors, including KLRK1/NKG2D, which is involved in target cell killing (Prajapati et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by scRNAseq data showing Klrk1 expression and citation to literature on NKG2D function.

claim: KILR effector CD8+ T cells show superior cytotoxic properties in vivo.
source: Since these cells show superior cytotoxic properties in vivo, suppression of their formation is probably a major mechanism of Treg-mediated self-tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo killing assay data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Treg depletion in polyclonal mice increased the frequency of KILR effector CD8+ T cells, but they were present at low numbers.
source: Although Treg deficiency increased the frequency of KILR effector CD8+ T cells, they were present at low numbers (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claim: The combination of IL-2 administration and antigenic stimulation efficiently induced KILR effector CD8+ T cells in OT-I mice.
source: Indeed, the combination of IL-2 administration and antigenic stimulation efficiently induced KILR effector CD8+ T cells in OT-I mice (Figure 6B–E), which were characterized by high GZMB and IL-7R expression, whereas the stimulation with IL-2 or antigen alone failed to induce the complete KILR phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: All three subsets (KILR, naïve, and effector) maintained the expression of their signature markers after adoptive transfer.
source: We observed that all three subsets maintained the expression of their signature markers (Figure 6F), documenting the stability of the KILR phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by competitive adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: KLRK1+ T cells induced by the combination of antigen and IL-2ic showed the most potent cytotoxic activity on per cell basis.
source: KLRK1+ T cells induced by the combination of the antigen and IL-2ic showed the most potent cytotoxic activity on per cell basis (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo killing assay data shown in Figure 6H and supplementary figures.

claim: A human CD8+ T-cell population expressing KILR signature genes was identified, constituting ~1-10% of all CD8+ T cells.
source: After removing MAIT cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K, cluster 6), we identified naïve, memory, and effector T cells, and the population expressing some KILR effector CD8+ T-cell signature genes such as NK markers (KLRD1, IFITM3, CD7) and IL7R (Figure 6I and J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1L, Supplementary file 2). Similarly to mouse KILR effector CD8+ T cells, this human T-cell subset was enriched for NK signature genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1M). Human KILR-like T cells constituted for ~1–10% of all CD8+ T cells (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of human CD8+ T cell atlas data shown in Figure 6I-K and supplementary figures.

claim: Human KILR-like T cells showed no signs of clonal expansion, but expressed rearranged αβTCR genes.
source: These cells showed no signs of clonal expansion, but expressed rearranged αβTCR genes, ruling out the possibility that these cells were NK cells or another non-T cell subset (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is supported by TCR analysis shown in Figure 6L.

claim: IL-2/JES6 in combination with doxorubicin slowed down the progression of BCL1 leukemia.
source: This IL-2ic slowed down the progression of the disease, when co-administrated with a chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin (Dox) (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7B and supplementary figures.

claim: The anti-tumor effect of Dox plus IL-2ic was dependent on CD8+ but not on CD4+ T cells.
source: This effect was dependent on CD8+ but not on CD4+ T cells, as revealed by antibody-mediated depletion of these subsets (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data with T cell depletion shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Depletion of CD4+ T cells improved the anti-tumor effect of Dox plus IL-2ic combinational treatment.
source: Depletion of CD4+ T cells even more improved the anti-tumor effect of Dox plus IL-2ic combinational treatment, presumably due to the depletion of Tregs, which could still limit IL-2 availability between the IL-2ic injections.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7B and inference about Treg depletion.

claim: The administration of IL-2ic without chemotherapy showed no therapeutic effect in BCL1 leukemia model.
source: The administration of IL-2ic without the chemotherapy showed no therapeutic effect (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a synergy between the IL-2 signals and the presentation of antigens released from tumor cells undergoing an immunogenic cell death (Obeid et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7B and citation to literature on immunogenic cell death.

claim: Mice treated with Dox and IL-2ic generated a large population of KLRK1+ T cells in BCL1 leukemia model.
source: Mice treated with Dox and IL-2ic, but not those treated with Dox alone or untreated, generated a large population of KLRK1+ T cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The frequencies of KLRK1+ CD49d+, KLRK1+ CD49d-, KRLK1+ IL-7R+, and KLRK1+ GZMB+ CD8+ T-cell subsets were significantly higher in the spleens of mice treated with Dox and IL-2ic than in control mice.
source: The frequencies of KLRK1+ CD49d+, KLRK1+ CD49d-, KRLK1+ IL-7R+, and KLRK1+ GZMB+ CD8+ T-cell subsets were significantly higher in the spleens of mice treated with Dox and IL-2ic than in the control mice (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C and supplementary figures.

claim: Combinational therapy of Dox plus IL-2/JES6 showed protective effects in B16F10 melanoma model.
source: We observed very similar protective effects of combinational therapy of Dox plus IL-2/JES6 in a B16F10 melanoma model (Figure 7D and E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by survival and tumor volume data shown in Figure 7D, E and supplementary figures.

claim: The spleens of mice treated with Dox and IL-2ic had much higher frequencies of KLRK1+ GZMB+, KLRK1+ CD49d+, and KLRK1+ CD49d- CD8+ T cells than untreated or Dox-only treated mice in B16F10 melanoma model.
source: The spleens of mice treated with Dox and IL-2ic had much higher frequencies of KLRK1+ GZMB+, KLRK1+ CD49d+, and KLRK1+ CD49d- CD8+ T cells than the untreated or Dox-only treated mice (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7F and supplementary figures.

claim: A large proportion of CD8+ T cells infiltrating the tumors in the Dox plus IL-2ic treated mice had the KLRK1+ CD49d- phenotype.
source: A large proportion of CD8+ T cells infiltrating the tumors in the Dox plus IL-2ic treated mice had the KLRK1+ CD49d- phenotype, whereas these cells were relatively rare in the untreated and Dox-only treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes shown in Figure 7G.

claim: KLRK1+ T cells in tumors of Dox + IL-2ic group expressed higher levels of IL-7R and GZMB than their counterparts in untreated or Dox-only treated mice.
source: Moreover, KLRK1+ T cells in tumors of Dox + IL-2ic group expressed higher levels of IL-7R and GZMB than their counterparts in untreated or Dox-only treated mice (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The Dox + IL-2ic therapy enhanced the anti-tumor immune response in a CD8+ T cell-dependent manner and induced large numbers of KLRK1+ CD8+ T cells.
source: Overall, the Dox + IL-2ic therapy enhanced the anti-tumor immune response in a CD8+ T cell-dependent manner and induced large numbers of KLRK1+ CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data from Figure 7 showing CD8+ T cell dependence and KLRK1+ cell induction.

claim: Tregs do not alter the antigen-affinity discrimination as they suppress both high-affinity and low-affinity CD8+ T cells.
source: We observed that Tregs do not alter the antigen-affinity discrimination as they suppress both high-affinity and low-affinity CD8+ T cells, which is in an apparent contrast with a previous study (Pace et al., 2012) concluding that Tregs suppress exclusively low-affinity T-cell responses.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data from Figure 2 showing Treg effects across different antigen affinities, contrasting with cited literature.

claim: The reduction of available IL-2 is the major mechanism of Treg-mediated tolerance of CD8+ T cells.
source: We have identified the reduction of available IL-2 as the major mechanism of Treg-mediated tolerance of CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including IL-2 signaling data and IL-2ic experiments.

claim: Strong exogenous IL-2 signals stimulate the expansion of Tregs and the expression of their effector molecules.
source: Strong exogenous IL-2 signals stimulate the expansion of Tregs and the expression of their effector molecules (Tomala and Kovar, 2016), which should enhance all their potential suppression mechanisms with the notable exception of IL-2 sequestration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature and experimental observation of Treg expansion with IL-2ic.

claim: IL-2/JES6 in combination with chemotherapy significantly prolonged the survival of tumor-bearing mice in two different tumor models in a CD8+ T-cell-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, IL-2/JES6 in combination with chemotherapy significantly prolonged the survival of tumor-bearing mice in two different tumor models in a CD8+ T-cell-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figure 7 showing survival benefits in BCL1 and B16F10 models.

claim: A strong sustained IL-2 signal potentiates antigen-induced CD8+ T-cell antitumor immunity and autoimmunity despite its concomitant stimulatory effects on Tregs.
source: Collectively, these results reveal that a strong sustained IL-2 signal, even if selective for IL-2Rα+ cells, potentiates antigen-induced CD8+ T-cell antitumor immunity and autoimmunity despite its concomitant stimulatory effects on Tregs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing IL-2ic effects on both autoimmunity and tumor immunity.

claim: A combinational therapy of in vitro expanded polyclonal Tregs and low-dose IL-2 was tested in patients with type I diabetes in a phase I clinical trial.
source: Recently, a combinational therapy of in vitro expanded polyclonal Tregs and low-dose IL-2 was tested in patients with type I diabetes in a phase I clinical trial (Dong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published clinical trial.

claim: The clinical trial authors did not observe a benefit of Treg plus IL-2 intervention for type I diabetes patients but reported an expansion of Tregs along with activated NK and cytotoxic CD8+ T cells.
source: The authors of the study did not observe a benefit of this intervention for the patients but they reported an expansion of Tregs along with activated NK and cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, which corresponds to our conclusions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the clinical trial results and comparison to the current study's findings.

claim: Antigen-stimulated CD4+ T cells are less sensitive to IL-2 signals than CD8+ T cells in vivo.
source: First, we show that antigen-stimulated CD4+ T cells are less sensitive to IL-2 signals than CD8+ T cells in vivo, which limits the potential impact of the IL-2 restriction on them.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Tregs lacking the high-affinity IL-2 receptor can still control the homeostasis of CD4+ T cells but not CD8+ T cells.
source: Second, it has been shown that Tregs lacking the high-affinity IL-2 receptor, implied in IL-2 sequestration, can still control the homeostasis of CD4+ T cells but not CD8+ T cells (Chinen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tregs suppress conventional CD4+ T cells by depleting their cognate peptide-MHCII from APC.
source: Third, it has been shown that Tregs suppress conventional CD4+ T cells by depleting their cognate peptide-MHCII from APC, which is not applicable for the suppression of MHCI-restricted CD8+ T cells (Akkaya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Self-reactive CD4+ T cells produce IL-2 locally attracting Tregs to their close proximity, which leads to suppression at least partially via limiting IL-2.
source: In contrast, a recent study proposed that self-reactive CD4+ T cells produce IL-2 locally attracting Tregs to their close proximity, which leads to the suppression of later phases of self-reactive T-cell activation at least partially via limiting IL-2 (Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent published study.

claim: Conventional effector T cells are characterized as IL-7R-, which is associated with their short lifespan.
source: The expression of IL-7Rα in KILR effector CD8+ T cells is striking as conventional effector T cells are characterized as IL-7R-, which is associated with their short lifespan (Joshi et al., 2007; Kaech et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on effector T cell characteristics.

claim: Antigenic stimulation together with activating antibodies to OX40 and 4-1BB TNF-family receptors induced IL-7R+ effector CD8+ T cells.
source: A previous study showed that antigenic stimulation together with activating antibodies to OX40 and 4-1BB TNF-family receptors induced IL-7R+ effector CD8+ T cells (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: OX40/4-1BB-induced IL-7R+ effector CD8+ T cells produced high levels of proinflammatory cytokines in an IL-7-dependent manner.
source: These cells produced high levels of proinflammatory cytokines in an IL-7-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: 4-1BB signaling has been shown to enhance IL-2 production and IL-2Rα expression in T cells.
source: Since 4-1BB signaling has been shown to enhance IL-2 production and IL-2Rα expression in T cells (Barsoumian et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2015), it is possible that those IL-7R+ effector cells were induced via a strong IL-2 signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and speculation about mechanism.

claim: The infection with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus induces a transient drop in Treg numbers.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the infection with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus induces a transient drop in Treg numbers (Schorer et al., 2020), which might alleviate the Treg-mediated suppression of virus-specific CD8+ T cells in the early phase of the immune response.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and speculation about consequences.

claim: KILR effector CD8+ T cells were not found in any scRNAseq dataset from the course of mouse infection.
source: However, we could not find KILR effector CD8+ T cells in any scRNAseq dataset from the course of mouse infection, suggesting that such KILR effector-inducing conditions would be rather rare.
evidence: This is based on analysis of existing datasets and inference about rarity of inducing conditions.

claim: Increased frequencies of KILR cells were found in the spleens and tumors in mice with cancer treated with Dox and IL-2ic.
source: On the other hand, we found increased frequencies of KILR cells in the spleens and tumors in mice with cancer treated with Dox and IL-2ic.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from tumor experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The antigenic stimulation in tumor-bearing mice was probably provided by tumor-associated antigens released from cancer cells undergoing immunogenic cell death induced by Dox.
source: The antigenic stimulation was probably provided by tumor-associated antigens released from cancer cells undergoing the immunogenic cell death induced by Dox (Obeid et al., 2007; Kim and Kin, 2021).
evidence: This is based on citations to literature on immunogenic cell death and inference about antigen source.
